entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jean de Corbeil (died November 1, 1318), Seigneur of Grez-sur-Loing, rose through the ranks of the French aristocracy to become a Marshal of France, a pivotal military appointment during the reign of King Philip IV "the Fair." His career, spanning the late 13th and early 14th centuries, placed him at the heart of the Capetian monarchy's efforts to consolidate royal power and assert its dominion over contested territories, particularly in the ongoing conflicts with England and Flanders. Corbeil's significance lies in his embodiment of the professionalizing military leadership that underpinned French expansionism and defense during a period of intense geopolitical flux in Western Europe.

His military career was marked by active participation in several key campaigns. Appointed Marshal of France in 1308, Corbeil had already distinguished himself in earlier engagements. He fought prominently in the Franco-Flemish War, including the disastrous Battle of the Golden Spurs in 1302, where, despite the French defeat, his experience would have been invaluable for subsequent tactical adjustments. He later played a role in the pivotal Battle of Mons-en-Pévèle in 1304, a French victory that temporarily reasserted Capetian authority over Flanders. Beyond these major battles, Corbeil served as a royal captain in various regions, including Poitou, demonstrating the Crown's reliance on experienced marshals to maintain order and enforce its will across the kingdom's diverse provinces. He was also involved in the early stages of French military interventions in the Iberian Peninsula, further illustrating the broad scope of his service.
